title: The Quiet Encore
subtitle: Stars Between the Strings · Chapter 37 of 40
content:
The last audience member had gone home, but Greg was still working.

He was coiling a cable when I found him. The Starwake stage stood empty, its lanterns dark except for the safety light near the steps. Someone had left a paper cup under the bench. The wind made it roll in small circles.

"Are we done?" I asked.

"Almost."

"That's what you said twenty minutes ago."

"Time is a mysterious concept to musicians."

He grinned without looking up.

Greg had agreed to play one set at the Listening Fair. He played beautifully. Then he'd helped carry chairs, checked the microphone, found missing keys and offered to stay until every piece of equipment was packed.

The actual cleanup volunteers were standing nearby, waiting for him to hand over the last two cables.

I touched his elbow.

"Greg, they're here."

He looked at the workers.

"Oh. Right."

Nola, the shift leader, held out her hand.

"We've got the equipment from here. That was the agreement."

"Sure, but I can help with—"

"Your shift ended."

He stopped and gave her the cable. She smiled.

"Thanks for the music. Go rest."

We walked to the safe bench along the pier. The western boards had passed inspection with posted limits. The strange low note beneath the supports hadn't sounded that evening; Fen's tide chart showed an ordinary tide. Beyond the lanterns, the sea moved in dark folds.

Greg sat and stared toward the empty stage.

"You were quiet during the last song," he said.

"I liked it."

"Was it too slow?"

"No."

"Too sad?"

"Greg."

He looked at me.

"Are you asking whether I liked the music, or whether I liked you?"

He laughed weakly.

"Probably both."

I sat beside him.

"I liked the music. I love you. I'm allowed to be quiet while I listen."

He smiled, then looked embarrassed.

"Everybody goes home when the music stops," he said. "I used to think if I kept the lights on long enough, no one would forget me."

"Is that why you keep doing everyone else's cleanup shifts?"

"Maybe."

"Does it help?"

He looked at his hands.

"No. Mostly it makes me tired and a little resentful nobody knows I'm tired."

"Have you told anyone?"

"I'm telling you."

I reached toward him, then paused.

"Want me close?"

"Yeah."

I moved closer. He put an arm around my shoulders, and we shared the blanket he'd brought for me.

"Did you bring one for yourself?" I asked.

"No."

"Then this one is ours for a while."

He tucked it around both of us.

Greg was generous with things he could offer without being asked. It took much more courage for him to admit he needed something. I recognized the habit. I had spent too many years hoping people would notice what I couldn't bring myself to say.

"Can I ask you something difficult?" he said.

"Yes."

"Do you ever worry I'm only happy when you need me?"

"Sometimes I worry you use being useful to avoid saying what you want."

"That's probably fair."

"What do you want tonight?"

He opened his mouth, then shut it.

"Not another concert."

"Good."

"Not a big talk about forever."

"Also good."

He looked almost shy.

"I want to sit here until the maintenance lights go out. Then maybe get something warm to eat. Have one night where neither of us needs to be interesting."

My chest tightened.

"I want that too."

"Wow. A perfectly matched set of glamorous wishes."

We laughed.

Nola finished locking the equipment shed and called a final goodnight. Greg thanked her without offering another shift. She had her own work and her own evening; we didn't have to become part of it.

We sat until the sea wind made my fingers cold.

"There's something else," Greg said.

I looked at him.

"I know you've got other places to go. Other people you love. We talked about ethical non-monogamy and your preference for polyamory when this first became serious. I meant it when I said I wanted to make room."

"I know."

"Sometimes when you leave for another date, I feel lonely. Then I tell myself I shouldn't, because I agreed."

"Loneliness doesn't mean you've broken our agreement," I said. "Neither of us promised never to feel afraid."

He let out a breath.

"Can I ask for next Sunday?"

"Yes. We can plan that. I have Moonroot work in the morning, but the afternoon is free. If it runs late, I'll tell you."

He nodded.

"I'd like that."

I rested my head against him. I could love someone without asking them to become the only person I loved. I could also take their loneliness seriously, without treating it as a demand to choose.

On the walk to the Starwake Door, Greg stopped to point out a tiny fish under the boardwalk, an upside-down lantern reflected in a puddle, and a scrap of paper caught on a nail.

"You're still working," I accused when he bent to pick up the paper.

"That was one piece of litter."

"An heroic intervention."

"Saved the entire pier."

I laughed.

At the late stall, Mara served soup so hot it made Greg burn his tongue. He insisted the temperature proved its artistic intensity. She told him to drink water and stop giving speeches in her doorway.

He obeyed.

We split the last roll. He asked if I wanted to go home with him. I said yes because I wanted to, not as a reward for his music.

At home, we left his guitar in its case. The evening did not need a soundtrack. He kissed me slowly, one hand warm against mine. I caught his sleeve and kissed him again. Later we closed the door and left the rest of the night private.

In the morning, I found him making breakfast.

No guitar. No microphone.

Just Greg trying not to burn toast.

"You look happy," I said.

"I am."

"Without an audience?"

"Especially without one."

He handed me a piece of toast. It was almost perfect.

I ate it anyway.

Later, Nola sent a note thanking the volunteers for honoring their scheduled shifts. Greg pinned it beside the old list of shows he thought he had to accept.

The old list stayed.

The new note went above it.
